newsitem.title: USA: One stock fund may not be enough.
newsitem.headline: One stock fund may not be enough.

text.p: Why do investors choose mutual funds instead of buying individual stocks directly? Diversification is probably the most important reason.

For as little as $1,000, and sometimes even less, you can buy a stake in a fund portfolio that includes scores or even hundreds of stocks. That means no single company's fortunes, or woes, can wreck your nest egg.

Trouble is, many funds don't offer as much diversification as investors may need. Sure, it's important to invest in a wide range of companies. But it's almost as crucial to spread your money out among different sectors of the stock market.

That doesn't mean you have to own shares in companies from every industry. But it does mean you should have a stake in the three major size categories in the stock market: small companies, mid-sized companies, and large companies.

If you don't invest in all three of those sectors, you risk getting left behind if the market suddenly shifts from the one sector that you do own. For example, from 1974 to 1976, shares of small-company stocks returned 24.4 percent annually, compared to only 7.7 percent for shares of large-company stocks, according to Ibbotson Associates, an investment research firm in Chicago.

Most so-called "diversified equity funds" concentrate their assets in shares of large companies. Even worse, funds that call themselves "mid-cap" or "small company growth" often give the lie to those names by tilting their holdings toward shares of bigger firms.

Often, funds shift toward larger company shares when blue chips are outgaining the stocks of smaller firms. As a result, the funds' shareholders are likely to miss some of the best opportunities to invest in small company shares at bargain prices.

Lately, small company shares have underperformed their larger cousins. Many smaller companies have reported disappointing earnings recently, causing investors to flock to blue-chip stocks. Some analysts believe that mid-sized and large company stocks will continue to dominate for the next year or so.

Regardless of which sector is likely to do best during the coming months, most fund investors should maintain holdings in all three sectors. You can do that for as little as $3,000 if you choose a fund such as Vanguard Index Total Stock Market (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum investment; no-load), which holds stock in more than 2,000 large, mid-sized and small companies that make up the Wilshire 5000 Index.

T. Rowe Price Spectrum Growth (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load) invests in a diversified group of other T. Rowe Price funds such as Growth Stock Fund and New Horizons that holds shares of large and small company growth stocks, growth-and-income shares and international securities.

Alternatively, you can choose the best funds in each sector. Among small company fund offerings, Managers Special Equity (800-835-3879; $2,000 minimum investment; no-load) has produced returns nearly 76 percent higher than similar funds, with less risk than the average small company fund.

Strong Schafer Value (800-368-1030: $2,500 minimum investment; no-load) typically holds shares of mid-sized companies with above-average earnings growth that trade at attractive valuations. Manager David Schafer has led the fund to a 17.8 percent average annual return during the past 5 years.

Finally, Harbour Capital Appreciation (800-422-1050; $2,000 minimum investment; no-load) is one of the better growth funds that invest in shares of larger companies, such as Microsoft and Walt Disney. Manager Spiros Segalas buys stable, well-managed firms with strong earnings growth.

If you're not sure whether a fund invests in small, mid-sized or large companies, you can get that information from Morningstar Mutual Funds, available at most libraries. The publication breaks down each fund portfolio into five categories by market capitalisation, also known as "market cap". Market cap equals the number of shares a company has outstanding multiplied by the price of the stock.

You also can get the same information by calling a fund's sponsor and asking about its market cap. You can put the numbers in perspective by comparing them to Morningstar's five categories: giant (market cap: greater than $25 billion); large ($5 billion to $25 billion); medium ($1 billion to $5 billion); small ($250 million to $1 billion) and micro (less than $250 million).
